cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Aviation – the flying or operating of aircraft.

p.em: Example: Modern aviation has made it possible to travel across continents in just a few hours.

cosy-blockquote.p: Passenger – a traveler on a public or private conveyance other than the driver, pilot, or crew.

p.em: Example: Every passenger on the plane must wear a seatbelt during takeoff and landing.

cosy-blockquote.p: Destination – the place to which someone or something is going or being sent.

p.em: Example: Paris is one of the most popular travel destinations in Europe.

cosy-blockquote.p: Jet lag – extreme tiredness and other physical effects felt by a person after a long flight across different time zones.

p.em: Example: It took her three days to recover from the intense jet lag after flying to Tokyo.

cosy-blockquote.p: Long-haul – traveling or transporting goods over a long distance.

p.em: Example: He prefers booking overnight long-haul flights so he can sleep through the journey.

cosy-blockquote.p: Eco-friendly ≠ pollutive – not harmful to the environment ≠ causing environmental damage or pollution.

p.em: Example: Traveling by train is highly eco-friendly, whereas flying is notoriously pollutive.

cosy-blockquote.p: Slow travel – an approach to travel that emphasizes connection to local people, cultures, and slow transit.

p.em: Example: She embraced slow travel by taking a scenic train journey across the countryside instead of flying.

cosy-blockquote.p: Baggage allowance – the amount of luggage a passenger is permitted to carry without paying an extra fee.

p.em: Example: The low-cost airline has a very strict baggage allowance of exactly ten kilograms.

cosy-blockquote.p: Frequent flyer – a person who travels regularly on aircraft, especially with a particular airline.

p.em: Example: As a frequent flyer, he receives complimentary access to the airport business lounge.

cosy-blockquote.p: Layover – a period of rest or waiting before a further stage of a journey.

p.em: Example: We had a six-hour layover in Dubai, so we decided to explore the terminal shopping area.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
How has modern aviation changed the way families stay connected across different continents?
★ Have you ever had to use aviation to visit a loved one who lives far away?

What is the most common complaint of a long-haul flight passenger regarding comfort and service?
★ When you are a passenger, how do you usually spend your time during a long flight?

Does reaching a distant destination very quickly make the travel experience feel less rewarding?
★ What is your dream travel destination that you hope to visit in the near future?

Why is physical jet lag such a strange, exhausting psychological experience for the brain?
★ How do you usually deal with or cure your jet lag after arriving in a new time zone?

How do you physically and mentally prepare for a exhausting, twelve-hour long-haul flight?
★ Have you ever taken a long-haul flight? What was the hardest part of the journey?

Is it genuinely possible for modern aviation to become eco-friendly, or is it destined to stay pollutive?
★ Do you feel guilty about the environmental cost of flying when you book a vacation?

Why is the philosophy of slow travel gaining so much popularity among stressed urban professionals?
★ Would you ever choose a slow, multi-day train journey over a quick two-hour flight?

Why are low-cost airlines so strict about their exact cabin baggage allowance guidelines?
★ Do you usually travel light, or do you always struggle with exceeding the baggage allowance?

How does being a frequent flyer alter your perspective on geography, borders, and cultural differences?
★ Do you consider yourself a frequent flyer, or do you travel only once or twice a year?

What is the best way to spend a long, boring layover in an unfamiliar international airport terminal?
★ Have you ever had a terrible or funny experience during an airport layover?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: collaborative task or visual analysis in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, work together on the following task:

cosy-blockquote.p: The Train Voyage Task: Imagine airplanes have been banned worldwide for environmental reasons. Work as a group to design a slow travel route from London to Beijing using only trains, ships, and cars. What countries would you cross? Present your slow-paced adventure itinerary!

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: 1-on-1 guided visual description and task response with teacher.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li: Imagine a world with absolutely no aviation-how would our global economy and remote supply chains survive?
Without planes, every international passenger would have to spend weeks traveling on ocean liners and trans-continental trains.
Reaching a distant destination would become a rare, once-in-a-lifetime achievement rather than a quick weekend plan.
The complete absence of planes would mean the end of physical jet lag, aligning our bodies with local geographic time.
Instead of booking quick weekend splurges, long-haul journeys would require deep, careful planning and months of free time.
A shift to trains and ships would make global tourism highly eco-friendly, drastically reducing atmospheric pollution.
The philosophy of slow travel would become a normal reality for everyone rather than a trendy lifestyle choice.
Without strict airport security and baggage allowance fees, packing would become much more relaxed and comfortable.
The prestigious concept of the frequent flyer would be replaced by slow, seafaring passengers sharing months-long voyages.
Instead of a quick airport layover, travelers would spend days resting in beautiful, historic train station hotels.

ul.li: Incorrect: We traveled by the plane last summer. → Correct: We traveled by plane last summer. ((Underlined error: when specifying a means of transport with 'by', do not use an article like 'the' or 'a'))
Incorrect: The jet lag made me to feel very tired. → Correct: The jet lag made me feel very tired. ((Underlined error: the causative verb 'make' takes a bare infinitive without 'to'))

Incorrect: I have been packing my luggage since two hours. → Correct: I have been packing my luggage for two hours. ((Underlined error: use 'for' to describe a duration of time, and 'since' for a specific starting point))
